questions.q: Intellectual Property Rights are generally justified/rationalised on the basis of which of the following, among others?
o: They serve no economic or social purpose
Incentivising creativity and innovation by granting creators/inventors exclusive rights for a limited period, in exchange for eventual public benefit/disclosure
They exist purely to restrict public access to information permanently
They apply only to physical, tangible property
questions.src: Settled IP theory — IP rights balance incentivising innovation/creativity (via exclusivity) against eventual public benefit (through disclosure, limited terms, and fair use exceptions)

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as a traditional/main form of Intellectual Property under Indian and international IP law?
o: Patents, Trademarks, Industrial Designs, Geographical Indications, Copyright and Neighbouring Rights
Only patents, with no other recognised category
Only copyright, since other forms are not legally protected
Physical real estate and movable goods
questions.src: Settled IP classification, per the syllabus itself — main forms include Patents, Trademarks, Industrial Designs, GIs, Copyright and Neighbouring Rights, alongside newer forms like plant varieties and layout designs

questions.q: Which of the following is recognised as a 'newer form' of Intellectual Property, distinct from the traditional forms?
o: Copyright
Trademarks
Plant Varieties Protection, Geographical Indications of newer categories, Layout Designs, and IP issues concerning Artificial Intelligence
Patents
questions.src: Settled IP classification, per the syllabus — newer/emerging forms of IP include plant variety protection, biotechnology-related IP, layout designs, and AI-related IP questions

questions.q: The Paris Convention (1883) is a foundational international instrument primarily concerned with:
o: Copyright protection exclusively
Protection of industrial property (patents, trademarks, industrial designs), establishing principles like national treatment and priority right
Only geographical indications
Only plant variety rights
questions.src: Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, 1883 — foundational treaty establishing national treatment and the right of priority for patents, trademarks, and industrial designs

questions.q: The Berne Convention (1886) is the foundational international instrument primarily concerned with:
o: Patent protection
Protection of literary and artistic works (Copyright), establishing principles including automatic protection without formal registration requirements
Trademark registration procedures only
Semiconductor layout designs exclusively
questions.src: Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, 1886 — foundational copyright treaty establishing automatic protection (no registration formality required) and national treatment

questions.q: The TRIPS Agreement (1994), administered under the WTO framework, is significant because it:
o: Abolished all national intellectual property laws
Established minimum standards for IP protection and enforcement that WTO member countries are obligated to implement in their domestic law, significantly influencing India's IP legislative reforms
Applies exclusively to developed countries
Deals only with agricultural patents
questions.src: Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) 1994 — sets binding minimum IP protection/enforcement standards for WTO members, a major driver of India's post-1994 IP law reforms (patents, copyright, trademarks)

questions.q: The Madrid Agreement (1891) and its associated Protocol (1989) primarily relate to:
o: International patent filing procedures
The international registration of trademarks, allowing an applicant to seek protection in multiple member countries through a single application filed with WIPO
Copyright duration harmonisation
Plant variety certification
questions.src: Madrid Agreement 1891 and Madrid Protocol 1989 — establish the international trademark registration system administered by WIPO, enabling single-application, multi-country trademark protection

questions.q: The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), 1970, primarily facilitates:
o: Automatic worldwide patent grant with no further national examination required

A unified international procedure for filing a single patent application that has effect in multiple designated member countries, streamlining (though not replacing) the process of seeking patent protection in each country
Only design registration
Copyright enforcement across borders
questions.src: Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) 1970 — provides a unified international filing procedure; substantive examination and grant remain within each designated national/regional patent office

questions.q: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright protection in India generally arises:
o: Only after formal registration with the Copyright Office, with no protection existing before registration

Automatically upon creation of an original work fitting within a protected category (literary, dramatic, musical, artistic work, etc.), without any mandatory registration requirement — registration is optional and serves an evidentiary purpose
Only for works published outside India
Only for works created by government employees
questions.src: Copyright Act 1957 (consistent with the Berne Convention's no-formality principle) — copyright arises automatically upon creation of an original qualifying work; registration under the Act is optional evidentiary proof, not a precondition for protection

questions.q: The 'Idea-Expression Dichotomy' in copyright law refers to the settled principle that:
o: Copyright protects abstract ideas themselves, preventing anyone else from ever using the same idea
Copyright protects the particular original expression of an idea, not the underlying idea, concept, method, or principle itself, which remains free for others to use
Copyright never protects any expression, only ideas
There is no distinction between ideas and expression in copyright law
questions.src: Settled copyright doctrine (recognised internationally, including under TRIPS Article 9.2) — copyright subsists in the original expression of ideas, not in the ideas/concepts/facts themselves, which remain in the public domain for others to independently express

questions.q: The 'Doctrine of Fair Use/Fair Dealing' as an exception to copyright infringement generally permits:
o: Unrestricted commercial exploitation of any copyrighted work without permission

Limited use of copyrighted material without the owner's permission for specified purposes such as private/personal use, criticism, review, research, or reporting of current events, subject to statutory conditions
Only use by the original author's family members
Complete reproduction of a work for any purpose whatsoever
questions.src: Copyright Act 1957, Section 52 (fair dealing exceptions) — permits limited use for specified purposes (research, criticism, review, reporting current events, educational use, etc.) without infringing copyright, subject to conditions

questions.q: Under general principles of copyright ownership, the 'author' of a work (the first owner of copyright, subject to exceptions like works made in the course of employment) is generally:
o: Always the government, regardless of who created the work
The person who actually creates the original work (subject to specific statutory rules for works made for hire/in the course of employment, where the employer may be the first owner)
Never entitled to any rights over their own creation
Only entitled to rights if the work is registered
questions.src: Copyright Act 1957, Section 17 — the author is generally the first owner of copyright, subject to exceptions (e.g., works created in the course of employment under a contract of service, where the employer may be the first owner absent contrary agreement)

questions.q: Remedies available to a copyright owner against infringement under the Copyright Act, 1957 generally include:
o: No civil remedies, only criminal prosecution
Civil remedies such as injunction, damages/accounts of profits, and delivery-up of infringing copies, in addition to criminal remedies (fine and/or imprisonment) for certain infringements
Only monetary compensation, with no possibility of an injunction
Remedies available only against government infringers
questions.src: Copyright Act 1957 — provides both civil remedies (injunction, damages, accounts of profits, delivery-up) and criminal remedies (fine, imprisonment) for infringement, giving rights-holders multiple enforcement avenues

questions.q: Under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a 'trademark' is generally defined to include a mark capable of:
o: Only three-dimensional shapes, excluding words or logos
Being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and may include shape of goods, packaging, and combination of colours
Only sounds, excluding any visual marks
Only marks registered outside India
questions.src: Trade Marks Act 1999, Section 2(1)(zb) — defines 'trade mark' broadly to include marks capable of graphical representation and distinguishing goods/services, extending to non-conventional marks like shape and colour combinations

questions.q: Under Section 27 of the Trade Marks Act 1999, a person generally CANNOT sue for statutory 'infringement' of a trademark if:
o: The trademark is famous and well-known
The trademark is not registered — however, the common law remedy of 'passing off' remains available to protect an unregistered mark's goodwill and reputation against misrepresentation
The infringer is a foreign company
The mark was registered more than 10 years ago
questions.src: Trade Marks Act 1999, Section 27 — statutory infringement action requires registration; unregistered marks are protected instead through the common law action of passing off, safeguarding goodwill against misrepresentation

questions.q: To succeed in a common law action for 'Passing Off', a claimant must generally establish the 'classic trinity' test, which requires proving:
o: Only that the defendant is a large company

Goodwill/reputation attached to the claimant's goods/services, misrepresentation by the defendant likely to deceive the public, and damage (or likelihood of damage) to the claimant's goodwill as a result
That the claimant's mark is registered somewhere in the world
Only that the two marks look visually identical, with no other requirement
questions.src: The 'classic trinity' test for passing off (established in Reckitt & Colman Products Ltd v Borden Inc, applied consistently in Indian courts) — goodwill, misrepresentation, and damage are the three essential elements

questions.q: A 'well-known trademark' under the Trade Marks Act 1999 generally receives:
o: The same protection as any other mark, with no special consideration

Broader protection extending beyond the specific goods/services for which it is registered/used, recognising that use of a similar mark on unrelated goods could still cause confusion or dilution given the mark's widespread reputation
No protection whatsoever unless separately registered in every product category
Protection only within the state where the company is headquartered
questions.src: Trade Marks Act 1999 — well-known marks receive enhanced protection beyond their registered goods/services classes, in recognition of their widespread reputation and the risk of consumer confusion or dilution even in unrelated categories

questions.q: Under the Designs Act, 2000, a registrable 'design' generally refers to:
o: The functional/mechanical working of an article

Features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament, or composition of lines/colours applied to an article, which appeal to and are judged solely by the eye (i.e., the aesthetic/visual appearance, not the functional aspect)
Any literary work reduced to writing
A trademark used on packaging
questions.src: Designs Act 2000, Section 2(d) — 'design' means features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament, or composition of lines/colours applied to an article, judged solely by the eye; purely functional features are excluded from design protection

questions.q: Under Section 11 of the Designs Act, 2000, registered design protection is initially granted for:
o: 10 years from the date of registration, renewable once for a further 5 years (maximum total protection of 15 years)
20 years from the date of registration, non-renewable
5 years, renewable indefinitely every 5 years
Permanent protection with no expiry
questions.src: Designs Act 2000, Section 11(1)-(2) (verified against the bare Act text via India Code and IP India's official site) — initial term of 10 years from registration, extendable once by a further 5 years on Form-3 application before expiry, giving a maximum total of 15 years

questions.q: Under the Patents Act, 1970, a patentable invention must generally satisfy which of the following core criteria?
o: Novelty, Inventive Step (non-obviousness), and Industrial Applicability (capable of industrial use)
Only that the inventor is an Indian citizen
Only that the invention has never been thought of before, with no other requirement
Only that the invention is expensive to produce
questions.src: Patents Act 1970 — the three core patentability criteria are novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability, consistent with TRIPS Article 27 and international patent law norms

questions.q: Under the Patents Act, 1970 (as amended), the standard term of patent protection in India, consistent with TRIPS obligations, is:
o: 10 years from the date of filing
14 years from the date of grant
20 years from the date of filing of the patent application
Indefinite, with no fixed term
questions.src: Patents Act 1970, Section 53 (as amended to comply with TRIPS Article 33) — standard patent term is 20 years from the date of filing of the application

questions.q: A granted patent confers upon the patentee the exclusive right to prevent others, without consent, from:
o: Only from discussing the invention academically
Making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing the patented product/process in the country of grant, for the term of the patent
Filing any future patents in other countries
Reading the published patent specification
questions.src: Settled patent law principle (Patents Act 1970, Sections 48) — a patent grants exclusive rights to prevent unauthorised making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing the patented invention

questions.q: 'Compulsory Licensing' under the Patents Act, 1970 refers to a mechanism by which:
o: The patentee is permanently stripped of all rights over the patent

The government/Controller may, in specified circumstances (e.g., reasonable requirements of the public not satisfied, patented invention not available at a reasonably affordable price), authorise a third party to manufacture/use the patented invention without the patentee's consent, subject to payment of royalty
A patent automatically becomes public domain after 5 years
Only the original inventor can ever manufacture the patented product
questions.src: Patents Act 1970, Sections 84-92 — compulsory licensing provisions allow the Controller to grant licenses to third parties in defined public-interest circumstances (e.g., inadequate availability, unaffordability), a TRIPS-compliant flexibility, notably invoked in cases like Natco Pharma v Bayer (2012)

questions.q: Under Section 3 of the Patents Act, 1970, which of the following is generally listed as something NOT considered a patentable 'invention'?
o: A genuinely novel mechanical device with an inventive step and industrial application
A mere discovery of a scientific principle, or the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance
A new industrial manufacturing process meeting all patentability criteria
A novel pharmaceutical compound satisfying all statutory requirements
questions.src: Patents Act 1970, Section 3 — lists exclusions from patentability, including mere scientific discoveries and (under Section 3(d)) new forms of known substances absent enhanced efficacy, a provision central to the landmark Novartis v Union of India (2013) case on pharmaceutical patents

questions.q: An applicant seeking patent protection in multiple countries for the same invention will typically consider using the PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) procedure primarily because it:
o: Guarantees automatic grant in all member states without further examination
Allows filing a single international application that preserves the applicant's priority date and delays the cost/complexity of entering the 'national phase' in each individual designated country
Eliminates the need to ever pay patent office fees
Is only available to citizens of the United States
questions.src: Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) procedure — a single international application streamlines the process and delays (but does not eliminate) the need for separate national-phase filings and examinations, while preserving priority date benefits

questions.q: In Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court rejected a patent for the beta-crystalline form of imatinib mesylate (Glivec) under Section 3(d), even though Novartis showed the new form had improved flow properties, better thermodynamic stability, and increased bioavailability compared to the earlier known form. Why did these improvements NOT satisfy Section 3(d)'s 'enhanced efficacy' requirement?
o: The Court held these physical/processing improvements (flow, stability, bioavailability) do not by themselves establish 'enhanced efficacy' — in the context of pharmaceutical substances, the Court interpreted 'efficacy' specifically as THERAPEUTIC efficacy (actual improved treatment effect), which Novartis had not demonstrated
The patent was rejected purely on procedural/filing-deadline grounds, unrelated to Section 3(d)
The Court found the drug had no medical use whatsoever
Bioavailability improvements are legally irrelevant to patents in every jurisdiction worldwide
questions.src: Novartis AG v. Union of India (SC 2013) — the Court's central holding: in the pharmaceutical context, 'efficacy' under Section 3(d) means specifically THERAPEUTIC efficacy, not mere physical/pharmacokinetic improvements (flow, stability, bioavailability); this precise distinction (which properties count vs don't) is the exact nuance that made this a landmark 'anti-evergreening' ruling protecting access to affordable generic medicines

questions.q: Company A has used an unregistered trademark 'ZENVIA' for its skincare products for 8 years, building substantial goodwill. Company B later registers 'ZENVIA' as a trademark for similar products and begins using it. Under Indian trademark law's settled principle regarding PRIOR USE vs registration, what is Company A's strongest available remedy?
o: Company A has no remedy since it never registered the mark

Company A can bring a common law action for PASSING OFF against Company B, since Indian trademark jurisprudence gives significant weight to prior continuous use and accumulated goodwill — a passing off action does not depend on registration, and courts have consistently protected genuine prior users even against a later registered proprietor in appropriate cases
Company A must first get its own registration cancelled before doing anything
Registration always defeats prior use with no exceptions whatsoever under Indian law
questions.src: Settled Indian trademark principle — passing off protects goodwill built through prior use independent of registration; Indian courts (reflecting the broader 'prior user' doctrine) have repeatedly protected genuine prior users' goodwill even against later registered proprietors, a nuance testing whether students understand passing off exists precisely BECAUSE registration is not the sole basis of trademark rights in India

questions.q: A university professor photocopies three chapters of a copyrighted textbook (which are essential prescribed reading) and distributes them to students enrolled in the course, without seeking the publisher's permission. Applying the settled framework for educational fair dealing exceptions under the Copyright Act 1957, is this likely to be treated as fair dealing?
o: Never — any reproduction for students is automatic infringement with no possible defence

Indian courts have recognised a reasonably generous scope for reproduction in the course of instruction/educational purposes under Section 52, particularly for genuinely educational, non-commercial use directly tied to prescribed coursework (as reflected in cases addressing photocopying for educational purposes) — though the specific extent (e.g., entire textbook vs excerpts) and commercial context of any photocopying service involved remain relevant factors courts weigh
Yes automatically, with no limits whatsoever on how much can be copied for any educational purpose
Only the original publisher's employees may ever reproduce educational content
questions.src: Copyright Act 1957, Section 52(1)(i) and related educational-use jurisprudence (reflecting the broader judicial approach seen in Indian cases on educational photocopying) — courts have shown a relatively generous approach to genuinely educational, non-commercial reproduction directly tied to coursework, while still weighing factors like the extent of copying and any commercial photocopying-service context involved
